I also should have monitored the electrical system more in flight but I'm not sure what that would have done as my photo verified there was no low voltage light.
ASRSN:2121367.s: The pilot ferried a Cessna from ZZZ to ZZZ3 after a reported battery fix but experienced progressive electrical failures, including G5 data bus loss and radio outages, likely due to an unverified alternator issue. The pilot executed a safe landing at ZZZ3 using light gun signals after losing all radio communication and partial flap extension.

ASRSN:2121376.n: On or about XA:30 PM on Day 0 I was conducting a flight for the company under Part 107 operations. I was tasked with gathering 'bird's eye view' imagery of the rooftop from 150 feet which I completed successfully. The other task was to capture 'perimeter' images of the roof eaves, which I successfully flew manually with the DJI Fly app. However, I second-guessed myself, and I had created a pre-programmed waypoint flight in the Litchi app to execute a sideways flight, capturing images at predetermined waypoints, in case my images from manual flight were unacceptable to the client. My errors were twofold: the first error was relying on an old satellite mapping image to plan my mission. The tree next to the church that I crashed my drone into had grown since the photographs were taken, and I was unaware of this, so the last waypoint on the mission did not stop short of the tree branches, but instead sent my drone sideways (the only flight direction in which collision avoidance does not work on this model)into the branches. My second error was forgetting that the Litchi app does not have a waypoint override panic mode like the DJI Fly app, where a programmed flight can be stopped by pulling the control sticks inwards and downwards to cause the drone to hover. By the time I remembered that the programmed flight must be stopped by tapping a button on my phone screen, the drone had already collided with the tree branches and become ensnared in the evergreen. The drone was flipped upside-down according to its IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit), and therefore the propellers could not be engaged to cause it to disentangle from the tree. I believed that the drone had fallen on the roof, and I called the church maintenance staff who arrived and looked on the roof using a ladder. They determined that the drone was still entangled with the tree branches and therefore not retrievable. We in fact could not see the drone in the branches, although the footage from the camera was still transmitting and showed a tangle of small twigs with sky beyond. Before the battery drained completely I downloaded the assets I had captured, communicated with the maintenance staff at the church about the event, and filed a claim with DJI for a 'flyaway'/unretrievable drone. The church maintenance staff confirmed that the tree would not need repair or remediation due to the crash, therefore the crash did not cause damages over $500USD. This is why I did not report the incident to the FAA or NTSB. A month later I was contacted by an individual who found the disabled and deactivated drone, and wanted a reward for its return. Not being able to afford a reward for them, I told them to return it to the manufacturer, as it had already been disabled/totaled by DJI. I therefore confirmed that the drone is not in the environment posing any kind of hazard due to its battery or otherwise. I hope that this report will fulfill any reporting obligation that I may be facing, but as far as I can tell from FAA CFR Part 107, I do not have an obligation to report the incident to them due to the low value of the damages incurred (none beyond the UAS itself). Corrective action taken is to reevaluate my mission planning procedure and never rely on satellite imagery for judging the position of foliage or any object that could pose an obstacle to UAS operation. Another corrective action taken is to re-read the manual for the Litchi app to remind myself of the procedure for stopping an automated waypoint flight.
ASRSN:2121376.s: A Part 107 drone pilot crashed a DJI drone into tree branches while executing a pre-programmed Litchi app waypoint mission at 150 feet. The collision occurred because outdated satellite imagery failed to show tree growth and the pilot could not manually override the automated flight in time.

ASRSN:2121377.n: We were flying an inspection of a section of power line. From the starting point I flew in reverse motion to follow the line to the end point. Near the midpoint of flight the sensor requested a yaw motion. I finished the mission, with 32% left on my batteries. I started home, not realizing my perception of the drone orientation was not correct. When I moved to come home, the motion was in an unexpected direction and I lost sight of the craft. Knowing I was at the max of 400ft AGL and well above any obstacles I used the distance from home in an attempt to return home. The batteries hit 20% which was our minimum setting. I was unaware the craft started descending when the batteries reached the minimum setpoint. I hit the return home button, the craft continued to descend into a tree approximately 1700ft from my launch point.
ASRSN:2121377.s: A pilot flying a drone for power line inspection lost visual contact due to incorrect orientation perception. The craft descended automatically at the 20% battery minimum and crashed into a tree 1,700 feet from the launch point.

ASRSN:2121382.n: While working X sector Y [sector] calls for a departure off ZZZ for ZZZ1. These departures are released on X sector freq. and are routed runway heading climbing to 030. I radar identify Aircraft X on departure and give them a 030 heading and then a climb to 040. There was a photo mission at 055 and wanted to avoid a TCAS and also was going to keep Aircraft X in the lower 039 MVA to be sequenced behind inbound traffic. Aircraft X did not climb very well at all. Climbing to only 028 over an estimated 5 miles of flight. I noticed the climb rate too late to avoid the MVA and gave the aircraft an immediate climb to 040 and then to 050. The aircraft quickly climbed above the MVA and landed uneventfully at ZZZ1 airport.Recommendation: In my time working traffic at ZZZ [TRACON] I've never seen a jet or turboprop aircraft perform so poorly with the exception of an emergency aircraft. I wasn't expecting nor would I have ever thought this would be an issue. I will have to pay more attention in the future or have the Y sector work them where they are used to dealing with their MVAs in that area.
ASRSN:2121382.s: Air Traffic Controller in Sector X issued climb clearances to departing Aircraft X, which climbed poorly to only 2,800 feet, risking Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA) violation. The controller issued immediate climb instructions to 4,000 and 5,000 feet, allowing the aircraft to clear the MVA and land uneventfully.

ASRSN:2121393.n: We arrived at aircraft and after completing my flows, I attempted to clean my oxygen mask as history has proven they are normally rather dirty and lint covered. I found the head of rivet at the bridge of the full face mask nose was missing. I then checked the 1st observers mask to verify its condition, and found the same problem with the mask. I then asked the FO to look at his mask. It had the exact same issue with the rivet head being broken off. Only the second observer's mask was fully operational. I contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control to report the situation. Multiple full face oxygen masks broken.Suggestions: The Company needs to have either or both Maintenance and the Pilot group clean and inspect the oxygen masks on the first flight of the day. When the Pilots were required to wear their oxygen masks when the other Pilot left the cockpit at altitude they normally clean and inspected the oxygen masks. Since the FAR change during COVID, primarily only Maintenance inspects the mask and they are only verifying that the retention harness is inflating within 3-seconds. Pilots are more likely to encounter a pressurization/smoke or fume event than an engine failure during their career, so both Flight Ops and Maintenance should ensure that the oxygen masks are fully functional. The Company should contact manufacturer to find if the mask is capable of dealing with a smoke/fume event or a depressurization event with the head of the rivet and/or if the rivet is completely missing. If so, then add an MEL so we can use the oxygen mask safely to get to a base or airport that it can be fixed or replaced.
ASRSN:2121393.s: Pilots discovered that three full-face oxygen masks had missing rivet heads at the nose bridge during pre-flight inspection, leaving only one operational. The crew reported the defect to Dispatch and Maintenance, suggesting that both Flight Ops and Maintenance should inspect masks daily to ensure functionality for potential smoke or depressurization events.

ASRSN:2121419.n: While at cruise at FL360 and as PM, aircraft started to rumble then entered at slow left bank for a few seconds, then a sudden left bank reaching about 25 degrees of bank. At this point the autopilot was disconnected and CA made corrective action to the right, while FO turned on fasten seatbelt sign and shadowed controls and monitored path. The plane then quickly banked to the right also reaching about 25 degrees of bank. 'Upset' was vocalized by FO and then CA, CA brought the plane to wings level while vocalizing 'push roll thrust stabilize'. Plane was then stable, autopilot re-engaged and ATC was notified of event. Left of course deviation and 2,000 feet descent was requested and granted. ATC notified us we were about 10 miles in trail of a company A319 same altitude, additionally it was almost a direct headwind aloft. After vector and altitude change the flight resumed uneventfully to destination.
ASRSN:2121419.s: During cruise at FL360, the aircraft experienced sudden uncommanded left and right banks, prompting the Captain to disconnect the autopilot and recover control. The crew stabilized the flight, notified ATC, and executed a 2,000-foot descent and course deviation to avoid a trailing A319 before resuming the flight.

ASRSN:2121431.n: This flight was a continuation of a divert to ZZZZ which originated in ZZZZ1. Prior to pushback we received a message from load planning telling us not to pushback until we received the final weights since ZZZZ personnel were not familiar with loading a 767. We received final weights after approximately 20 minutes after which we pushed back and started engines. Shortly after starting engines we received a message from both Dispatch and load planning that we not takeoff due to a possible large cargo weight error. We ultimately returned to the gate, and the cargo weight was confirmed to be more than 28,000 lbs heavier. While at the gate, we also received a planned dangerous goods message that we had not received prior to the previous pushback. Load planning eventually corrected both the cargo weight error and confirmed dangerous goods were on the aircraft. The flight departed without further issues. Departing ZZZZ, we had a weight restriction and the company was trying to maximize payload. We had a discussion with dispatch about performance departing Runway XX with a tailwind and came up with an appropriate weight and performance solution. Arriving at the departure end of the runway, the tailwind component had increased and we were no longer with in performance weight to take off and were around 5000 lbs too heavy. We asked ATC for a departure off of Runway XY and were told the delay would be 1 hour and 15 minutes. We communicated this to Dispatch and the decision was made to return to the gate and remove cargo. We received a message stating that the DG had been off loaded via a Final Dangerous Goods message.
ASRSN:2121431.s: The crew of a 767 at ZZZZ returned to the gate twice due to a 28,000 lb cargo weight error and an increased tailwind exceeding performance limits. After offloading cargo and dangerous goods, the flight departed without further issues.

ASRSN:2121455.n: During descent on the ZZZZZX arrival, we noticed a strong tailwind would challenge the FMGC to meet crossing restrictions. My attention was distracted by crossing, I did not see the cabin altitude issue until First Officer (FO) pointed it out, at about 24,000 feet. The cabin altitude was already at 9,500. As pilot monitoring (PM), I asked for and received an expedited clearance to 15,000 and relief from the 210 kt. speed assigned by ATC previously. It became apparent the the cabin altitude would exceed 10,000 feet about the time we passed 16,000 feet. We received an ECAM for off schedule descent I believe. We ran the ECAM, and observed the delta p was zero. The safety relief valve was open on the pressurization page. I [requested priority handling]. FO disconnected the Autopilot and auto thrust to further expedite our descent. We caught the cabin at around 11,000 feet. I contacted the purser, confirming that the passenger oxygen had not deployed. We were cleared for approach to Runway XXL. I had not pulled landing data for that runway. Uneventful approach and landing after 10;0000 feet.
ASRSN:2121455.s: During descent on the ZZZZZX arrival, the crew encountered a cabin altitude issue reaching 9,500 feet at 24,000 feet due to a pressurization failure with zero delta P. They expedited descent to 15,000 feet, caught the cabin altitude at 11,000 feet without oxygen deployment, and completed an uneventful landing.

ASRSN:2121476.n: While at cruise a passenger in seat XX had their laptop fall through a gap between the seat and the sidewall. Neither the Purser nor First Officer were able to locate the laptop, and it appeared to have fallen into the cargo pit area along the sidewall. After discussing the situation Dispatch, Maintenance Control, and the Chief Pilot, a decision was made to divert the aircraft to ZZZZ Airport. The decision was made because the laptop was inaccessible to the crew in the event of a battery fire over the ocean. The diversion to ZZZZ resulted in an uneventful overweight landing. The laptop was retrieved in the forward cargo pit sidewall by maintenance. The flight was unable to continue due to crew rest legalities and the flight from ZZZZ to ZZZ [airport] was cancelled. The flight operated the next day. Near the end of my rest break, the lead Flight Attendant opened the curtain and said he needed to brief me on a situation. I exited the bunk and he informed me that the passenger in seat XX had lost her laptop in the gap between the wall and the sidewall. He said he had alerted the flight deck and that the other First Officer had come out to investigate. He requested I look too as more sets of eyes might help. I checked around the seat and examined the gap. While there is normally secure gap filler there, the gap filler was loose. I examined the area and noticed what appeared to be a vent / deep cavity that clearly went lower than the cabin floor. I returned to the flight deck after securing the rest area (seat 1A). We all talked it over and elected to divert as we did not know the location nor condition of the laptop (we were concerned about a battery fire while over the middle of the ocean). The other two pilots already consulted dispatch and maintenance control. We originally planned to go to ZZZZ1 but dispatch requested we go to ZZZZ as they were better able to accommodate us. We checked landing performance, the overweight landing checklist, weather, and the diversion guide. The Captain made a PA to inform the passengers of the situation. We landed normally in ZZZZ (fire trucks were dispatched because of our over weight condition, not at our request). The BTMS (Brake Temperature Monitoring System) never exceeded 4. After some time, the laptop was recovered by local maintenance from behind a panel in the cargo pit. We ran out of duty time and were forced to deplane / have the passengers spend the night in ZZZZ.
ASRSN:2121476.s: During cruise, a laptop fell through a loose gap filler into the cargo pit, prompting a diversion to ZZZZ Airport due to potential battery fire risks over the ocean. The aircraft performed an uneventful overweight landing, the laptop was recovered by maintenance, and the flight was cancelled due to crew duty time limits.

ASRSN:2121544.n: I was the relief pilot of the flight from ZZZ to ZZZZ1 on Day 0, and assumed the role of Pilot Flying once I returned to the flight deck. While in cruise about 15 minutes from Waypoint 1 a FIRE FWD CARGO Master Warning and fire bell activated. I continued flying the aircraft after announcing 'My Aircraft' while the First Officer (FO) ran the Checklists. We sidestepped 5nm to the left of our route and [priority handling was requested]. We initiated a left turn towards ZZZZ after contacting company and ZZZ [Center]. After the aircraft was secured, weather was obtained and the pertinent people notified, I called the Captain whom was on their rest period during the event, by this time the FO had assumed Pilot Flying duties and I briefed the Captain on the situation, weather and plan. They then occupied the left seat and Flight Attendants were briefed about our situation and prepared the cabin for a precautionary landing at ZZZZ. The Fire Warning message was present during the majority of the event after the completion of the checklist. We came to the conclusion that we needed to jettison fuel since we were going to be overweight and we coordinated and attempted to jettison fuel twice but the system failed to activate, We then decided to proceed with an overweight landing. While FO flew the airplane, I ran landing assessments and provided latest weather for ZZZZ. Our landing weight was approximately 481,000. A normal approach and landing was performed on Runway XX and the aircraft was inspected by Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF). While taxiing to a parking location the FIRE warning returned, ARFF escorted the aircraft and positioned themselves around the aircraft in case they were needed. We deplaned passengers and crew safely after everything was secured and coordinated with airport personnel.
ASRSN:2121544.s: The relief pilot and First Officer managed a forward cargo fire warning during cruise, diverting for an overweight landing after fuel jettison failed. The aircraft landed safely at ZZZZ with ARFF escort, and the fire warning reappeared during taxi before all passengers and crew deplaned safely.

ASRSN:2121545.n: Runway 28L PAPI is so dim that it is unusable from first sighting to the ground. Cannot tell whether the lights are red or white. Better to have it decommissioned than to use in its current state so that it doesn't cause confusion and distraction. Bad equipment. Replace or repair the Runway 28L PAPI.
ASRSN:2121545.s: A pilot reported that the Runway 28L PAPI lights were too dim to distinguish red or white from first sighting to the ground. The reporter attributed this to bad equipment and recommended decommissioning, replacing, or repairing the system to prevent confusion.

ASRSN:2121562.n: FO was flying during ATC directed go around in IMC. Initiated climb at 1,400 feet AGL, was direct to climb to 4000 feet and turn left to heading 270. Climbed to 1900 feet AGL in turn and started cleaning up the airplane as it accelerated. Noticed we were accelerating quickly and not climbing then a decent was initiated. Noted to FO to pull back because we were descending. Decent rate increased quickly and I took the airplane as the gpws said pull up pull up". Arrested the decent initiated a climb approximately 1400 feet AGL. As we approached 4000 feet gave airplane back to FO and turned autopilot on. Continued on downwind to return to airport. Cause: Complacency in go around procedure contributed in confusion in maneuver Suggestions: Discipline in procedure practice and anticipation." Tower told us to go around due to another aircraft slowing early and loss of spacing. We were IMC and were told to turn to 270 degrees and climb to 4000. It caught me off guard and the go around happened very fast and we were both scrambling to accomplish it. When I hit the TOGA button the nose came up more aggressively than I expected and my natural reaction was to reduce the angle of pitch. I over controlled and the aircraft descended a few hundred feet and the Captain called out my error and I started climbing again. We got a sink rate call, but no pull up annunciation. No exceeded parameters were evident besides the sink rate.Cause: High workload, over controlled on pitch. Low frequency of performing go around makes the event more work than it needed to be at the time.Suggestions: I am going to review missed approach procedures every time I perform an approach. My missed approach cadence was disjointed and sloppy from lack of use and I am going to tighten it up.
ASRSN:2121562.s: Two pilots experienced a rapid descent during an IMC go-around due to high workload and over-controlling pitch after an unexpected ATC instruction. The Captain took control to arrest the descent following a GPWS warning, and the aircraft returned to the airport without exceeding parameters.

ASRSN:2121567.n: We were flying in a non radar environment, our radar was not depicting any weather in front of us and we were skimming the tops of some clouds. The clouds kept rising and we went inside eventually, immediately after penetration, we encountered severe turbulence, hail and lightning. The autopilot disconnected and I took over the airplane. We had airspeed fluctuate by 70 to 90 knots and altitude fluctuate between FL370 and FL 390 (we were cruising initially at FL380). The Captain [requested priority] and we took evasive action to exit the weather. Cause: This was my first time conducting a flight in a non-radar environment. And I was hesitant to turn away from the weather. Since the radar was not depicting anything, I backed myself into a corner.Suggestions: Next time, I will avoid the weather and not hesitate.
ASRSN:2121567.s: The pilot reported that while cruising at FL380 in a non-radar environment, the aircraft entered severe turbulence, hail, and lightning after penetrating rising clouds. The autopilot disconnected, causing significant airspeed and altitude fluctuations, which the pilot attributed to hesitation in avoiding weather due to a lack of radar depiction.

ASRSN:2121721.n: I was on my break in the bunks when the purser notified us we would be landing imminently due to a suspected fire in the cargo hold and [priority handling] had been requested onboard. The fire indicators had been going on and off in the flight deck for the cargo which initiated setting off the extinguishers and other cooling measures on the aircraft. The IFE (In Flight Entertainment) and other electronic controls were not working due to overheating. We were told there was a possibility of a ditching as the weather was too poor in ZZZZ1 to land there and they weren't sure what our options were. Meanwhile the galley was secured and power turned off. It was then decided we were to land in ZZZZ as a precautionary landing. The pilots informed the passengers that there was signs of smoke in the cargo and we would be diverting to ZZZZ and landing in 25 minutes. The crew prepares the cabin for landing as usual and took our jump seats. Upon landing [priority handling] vehicles were there and inspected the aircraft for probably a half hour. I smelled smoke but later was informed it could have been from the cargo extinguishers. They couldn't detect any heat from the outside so the aircraft was deemed unnecessary to evacuate. Then we parked the aircraft and had to wait about another half hour for any busses to arrive to deplane the passengers cabin by cabin to get in the busses. That took probably an hour. Then the crew deplaned. We sat on the bus for probably another half hour and firefighters came on saying they had only found evidence of condensation at that point, no fire. We were told we would not be getting back on that aircraft and our new plan was to lay over for the day and take the passengers in a new plane to ZZZZ2 at XA:00 pm, lay over for 28 hours and ZZZZ3 back to ZZZ (and they reflected that). Customs agents weren't there quite yet so the customs process took a very long time. I believe we got to the airport hotel at XB:45am. We were given minimum rest. We were told pickup was XB:30pm. There were very few food options around. I didn't hear anything from anyone until about XB:15pm the purser called my room informing me we were staying the night and leaving in the morning and he would give me more info shortly. 10 min later the FO called my room and said we were leaving tonight and come downstairs asap. At this time I found out the passengers had been flown to ZZZ1 earlier in the day in a plane flown in from ZZZ1. We all went to the airport where customs had gone home so we had to be escorted through the airport and then driven 4 at a time to the plane where maintenance was still working and they were still taking the cargo off. I was not asked if I was willing to work the original plane we had flown in. During that time a cargo pod of okra was taken out of cargo that was smoking and smoldering and hot to the touch. The pilot went out to investigate but it had been taken away. After probably an hour and a half on the aircraft I think we took off for ZZZ1 around XC:30 in the morning. Landed in ZZZ1 around XE:30 or XF:00 am where we went through customs and went to the hotel shuttle area to then be told there weren't enough rooms at the hotel so the captain called hotel limo and we split into two groups. We had minimum rest. At XE:00 pm we took the shuttle to ZZZ1 and we deadheaded back to ZZZ. There was someone from flight service who met the plane. Other than that I have never been called by the company or union to be checked in with.
ASRSN:2121721.s: Cabin crew reported a suspected cargo fire on an aircraft, causing IFE failure and a diversion to ZZZZ for a precautionary landing. Investigation later revealed a smoking, smoldering cargo pod of okra, leading to passenger rebooking, extended layovers, and minimum rest for the crew.

ASRSN:2121732.n: During cruising while doing the service the front of coach was 85 degrees and temp wouldn't go down. We informed the flight deck and as they tried to help some crew members complained of not feeling well. I felt dizzy and a slight irritation in airways. The CO2 sensor alarm Passengers and crew noticed a mild strange chemical smell. CO2 smoke alarm went off on both crew rest cabins. The Captain informed us then the passengers that we were returning to ZZZ. At the time we were around ZZZZ. Suggestions: I'm unaware of the existence of CO (Carbon Monoxide) detectors in the cabin or flight deck. I know there are CO2 sensors. If not available I'd like to see them installed.No real training or guidance on carbon monoxide poisoning other than generalized fumes event.No emphasis on CO awareness.
ASRSN:2121732.s: Cabin crew reported dizziness, airway irritation, and a chemical smell during cruise when cabin temperature rose to 85 degrees and CO2 alarms activated in crew rest areas. The Captain returned the aircraft to ZZZ, and the reporter noted a lack of CO detectors and specific training for carbon monoxide poisoning.

ASRSN:2121751.n: Aft cargo door explosively opened on takeoff roll. Takeoff aborted.
ASRSN:2121751.s: The aft cargo door explosively opened during the takeoff roll, causing the crew to abort the takeoff.

ASRSN:2121761.n: The Aft cargo door unexpected opened on initial takeoff roll.This occurred at aprox 45KiasThe takeoff was then promptly aborted.There were no injuries.
ASRSN:2121761.s: The aft cargo door unexpectedly opened at approximately 45 KIAS during the initial takeoff roll, prompting an immediate aborted takeoff. The incident resulted in no injuries.

ASRSN:2121771.n: I was instructor pilot in [a light aircraft] doing a left downwind departure from home airport with my learner who seeks to complete a flight review. At our airport, left downwind departures are common off the north-facing runway. We leveled off at pattern altitude which is 1200 MSL (1000 above airport elevation), leaving room for overflights that should maintain at least 1700 MSL until well clear of our traffic pattern.Learner and I observed conflicting traffic coming from our front-left on our ADS-B In display just 200 feet above our altitude, then 100 feet above, close to center-punching us if we did not make a change. Before we could pick the other aircraft up visually, I instructed my learner to make an immediate descent to try to provide some vertical separation. We then saw the other aircraft just a couple of hundred feet ahead of us crossing at right angle to our downwind flight path left-to-right, roughly 200 feet above us.I took a screenshot of the Foreflight display on my iPhone in order to capture offending aircraft's callsign. I then looked it up on Flight Aware and was able to see their flight path and altitude exactly as I just described. I shared all the information with our chief flight instructor, who then said he would call the flight school that offending aircraft belonged to, and discuss the event.
ASRSN:2121771.s: An instructor pilot and learner in a light aircraft on left downwind at 1200 MSL observed conflicting traffic 100–200 feet above on ADS-B In. The instructor initiated an immediate descent to avoid a near mid-air collision with an aircraft crossing their path, later sharing flight data with the chief instructor for follow-up.

ASRSN:2121781.n: Day 0Aircraft Dassault Falcon 50, Aircraft XCaptain Person A.SIC Person B While flying enroute from ZZZ1 to ZZZ aircraft experienced a rapid cabin depressurization.Rapid depressurization of cabin occurred at approximately XA:40z, 32 minutes into flight (take off time XA:08z). Location approximately 5NM south of ZZZ2 airport. Altitude FL350+ during climb, on autopilot, with intended level off at FL360. Speed approximately M0.78. No notable thud or bang sounds heard. CABIN warning light illuminated, ears popped and cabin oxygen masks self deployed. Captain (PNF) and SIC (PF) donned oxygen masks, Captain assumed controls (now PF). Captain initiated [priority handling] descent. Captain and SIC each made [priority handling] radio calls in the blind (due to headset removal for oxygen mask donning) to center [requesting priority handling] descent. Transponder code XXXX squawked, ATC communications re-established. Clearance to 14,000 feet assigned, revised to 10,000 feet.Event communication with company established. Route change to ZZZ3 requested and received from ATC. Remainder of flight uneventful at 10,000 feet. CABIN light extinguished at XB:12. Visually flew RNAV XX approach route and landed at ZZZ3, 20:35z. Aircraft delivered and parked at maintenance facility.Flight was for purpose of repositioning, no passengers on board. Aircraft was parked outside overnight prior to flight, in rain. Water drops were noted inside Aft Compartment during pre-flight inspection.On the previous day, this aircraft was flown at flight levels, by this crew with no pressurization anomalies observed.As of Day 1. Pressurization controller suspected cause.
ASRSN:2121781.s: The crew of a Dassault Falcon 50 experienced rapid cabin depressurization at FL350+ during climb, triggering oxygen mask deployment and an emergency descent to 10,000 feet. The aircraft landed safely at ZZZ3, with the pressurization controller suspected as the cause.

ASRSN:2121786.n: Following a short local personal VFR flight I was maneuvering in Class E airspace @ 3,000' AGL in the vicinity of a popular VFR reporting location ZZZ1 in anticipation of an eventual VFR approach and landing at ZZZ. I was monitoring ZZZ Tower in preparation for contacting them for entry into their Class D airspace. While positioning my aircraft for my arrival my ADSB suddenly depicted a traffic conflict alert indicating a high-speed target approaching my position. It seems I received very little warning possibly due to the approaching aircraft's relatively high-speed (est. @ 220 kts?) and the 8-nm scale being depicted on my moving map display. At about this same time the ZZZ Tower transmitted in the blind to my specific aircraft that they observed a potential traffic conflict requiring my evasive action. Since I was already taking such action I replied that I had the aircraft in sight and was adjusting my course/altitude to avoid conflict. The aircraft (an Company X A319) passed below and behind me and proceeded to land straight-in on ZZZ's RW XX. I subsequently requested and received a ZZZ Tower clearance for entry into the Class D airspace for a landing on RW XY.Observations: 1.) The ADSB traffic alert system works well and provides very useful traffic positional and alert information. 2.) The ZZZ Tower personnel were very observant in providing me with the timely traffic alert -- this is particularly true when one considers that I had not yet established communication with them for an ATC clearance into their Class D airspace.Suggestion: Over recent years ZZZ has experienced a significant increase in air traffic by medium-size air carrier aircraft (e.g., A319, B737, etc.). This increase has been well managed by tower, the airport admin, and the pilot community. In light of this increased air carrier traffic perhaps we need to reemphasize to the pilot community some of the more frequently utilized low-altitude approach/departure routing flown by these larger aircraft.
ASRSN:2121786.s: A VFR pilot at 3,000' AGL near ZZZ received an ADS-B alert and a blind traffic warning from ZZZ Tower regarding a high-speed Company X A319. The pilot executed evasive maneuvers, allowing the A319 to pass below and behind before the pilot received clearance to land on RW XY.

ASRSN:2121788.n: We were flying to ZZZ from ZZZ1 and at the top of our climbout the right engine shut down without warning. After this happened we [requested priority] and asked to turn around and return to ZZZ1. Due to how the right engine shut down we decided not to attempt a restart and continued back to ZZZ1 while descending. Due to our height above ground and mountainous terrain we decided a drift down to ZZZ1 would be the best course of action. We landed at ZZZ1 single engine without incident and parked the aircraft. We departed ZZZ1 going to ZZZ. At the top of climb the right engine shut down without any indication. When this happened we [requested priority] and turn towards ZZZ1. We choose not to restart the engine not knowing why it shut down happened and continued a drift down back to ZZZ1 would be the best course of action. We landed single engine without incident and parked the aircraft.
ASRSN:2121788.s: Pilots reported an uncommanded right engine shutdown at the top of climbout during a flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. They requested priority, elected not to restart the engine, and executed a drift down to land safely at ZZZ1 single-engine without incident.

ASRSN:2121793.n: -At SMQ, Runway 30 is generally favored -ASOS indicated that Runway 12 was slightly favored (20010KT)-After switching to the CTAF, one other aircraft indicated they were practicing the RNAV for Runway 12-I set up to overfly the field at 2,000 ft. and enter the downwind for Runway 12-On the CTAF, I realized there were two other aircraft that doing radio calls for Runway 30-I then set up for a crosswind entry for Runway 30 instead-While I was figuring out how to transition from Runway 12 to Runway 30, I missed that there was an aircraft on the upwind for Runway 30-My crosswind CTAF call and entry was late and cut in front of the other aircraft on the upwind for Runway 30-To prevent recurrence: 1) I need to better multi-task a change in pattern entry and continue to monitor the CTAF, 2) need a better way for everyone at an uncontrolled airport to use the same runway and coordinate changing the runway when the wind shifts
ASRSN:2121793.s: The pilot at uncontrolled SMQ switched from a planned Runway 12 approach to a Runway 30 crosswind entry due to wind and traffic, but missed an aircraft on upwind. This resulted in a late entry that cut in front of the other aircraft, prompting the pilot to cite poor multi-tasking and a lack of coordination for runway changes as causes.

ASRSN:2121822.n: On this night a drone show of, what was found out later, 500 drones conducted an unauthorized show .64 NM northwest of the ZZZ VOR. The tower was never made aware of the show. The controller working then Local Control (LC) 2 position was the first to notice the show. The controller working the helos advised the 2 that were on the tour of the show. One helo had to climb to 3,300 feet MSL to avoid the show. I was working TMU and told the controller working helos to not let any more helos depart due to safety concerns. The Police helicopter was out on patrol and provided assistance by getting the tower the number to the Hotel Security, where the drone show was being performed. After sometime the controller in charge was able to get in contact with someone from the hotel and they advised that the drone show was done for the evening. We then allowed for tours to continue. After further research, we found a NOTAM pertaining to the the drone show. The NOTAM was for a 12 hour time period and an altitude of SFC-400 feet AGL. There was no other information available such as specific times or contact information. The controllers in the tower were left in the dark about the entire show. The drones also appeared to go higher than 400 feet AGLWhomever approved this drone show should have coordinated with the tower. A NOTAM is not sufficient enough information for us to work with. There needed to be contact information for the drone show operator. The operator should have been instructed to call the tower for final approval to launch the show. There should have been outreach to all the helicopter operators about the drone show. The ball was seriously dropped on this and we should consider ourselves very lucky that there was not an accident. While working Local Control (LC) 2, I noticed what appeared to be a UAV show west of the field, near the airport. The show was not coordinated with the controller in charge nor where any controller made aware of this event. Aircraft X was on a tour route under the control of LC1 and the aircraft requested to climb due the UAVs. Upon research, it was determined that a NOTAM had been issued for the UAV show but the controllers working the shift where never briefed on the time, altitude, location or impact to the operation of the event. The event lasted approx 10 min as all helicopter operations were haulted until it could be determined what the actual show was. It appeared the UAV show was coordinated with management prior to the event and approved.Management, when made aware of events that may have any impact on the operation, should brief the controllers, especially the controllers working during the event.
ASRSN:2121822.s: An unauthorized drone show near the ZZZ VOR forced a helicopter tour to climb to 3,300 feet MSL and halted all helicopter operations. Although a NOTAM existed, controllers were not briefed on the event, causing a safety conflict that required police assistance to resolve.

ASRSN:2121885.n: Arriving in to BOI, in VMC conditions we cross IF DIKAC (RNAV 28L Zulu) expecting the visual approach to 28L. ATC asks if we have visual contact with Company aircraft ahead that was on left downwind for 28L. Both Captain and I agree that we have the aircraft to follow in sight. ATC clears us for visual approach, additionally to follow the aircraft ahead. I loaded 4,000 feet into MCP (Mode Control Panel) altitude preselect (I was expecting to intercept FAC outside FAF HOBSI), I began descent and adjusted pattern to follow aircraft ahead. For a moment I lost contact with traffic ahead and verbalized to that fact. Both Captain and I reacquired visual contact with the aircraft. Reacquiring the traffic cause a distraction. Aircraft was descending towards 4,000 feet, at approximately 4,200 feet GPWS issued 'caution terrain' one time. I disengaged automation and corrected altitude. TDZE is lower than general close in surrounding terrain. I had visual terrain contact at all times, however, 4,200 feet MSL at about 3-5 NM SE of HOBSI FAF resulted in a GPWS caution. I corrected altitude, maintained appropriate following distance, intercepted the approach course. We configured per Company SOP, established stable flight for descent and landed the aircraft. Captain and I debrief the situation during post flight discussion. The approach plate possibly led me to an inaccurate understanding of terrain risks outside of the final approach fix HOBSI. The profile view only presents the minimum crossing altitude at HOBSI whereas the plan view issues multiple crossing restrictions at fixes along the approach course. Hindsight: looking at the approach plate again, knowing I was going to be extended VFR downwind for traffic, I would have looked at those waypoint's further out and their associated crossing altitudes. I would have selected a higher altitude in the MCP. Arriving into BOI, in VMC conditions we cross IF DIKAC (RNAV 28L Zulu) expecting the Visual Approach to 28L. ATC asked if we had visual contact with Company. Cleared visual approach and instructed to follow the aircraft ahead. PF loaded 4,000 feet into MCP (Mode Control Panel) Altitude preselect (I was expecting to intercept FAC outside FAF HOBSI). PF began descent and adjusted pattern to follow aircraft ahead. Visual contact with traffic ahead was lost by PF. PM started to help PF re obtain the visual. Both Captain and PF re-acquired visual contact with the aircraft. The task of re-acquiring the traffic cause a distraction. Aircraft was descending towards 4,000 feet, at approximately 4,200 feet GPWS issued 'Caution Terrain' one time. PF disengaged automation and corrected altitude. TDZE is lower than general close-in surrounding terrain. Aircrew had visual terrain contact at times. The approach was continued after responding to the terrain caution. The approach plate possibly led Aircrew to an inaccurate understanding of terrain risks outside of the Final Approach Fix HOBSI. The Profile View only presents the minimum crossing altitude at HOBSI. The Planview issued multiple crossing restrictions at fixes along the approach course. Hindsight: there was a notice sent out months prior alerting Aircrews of this possible problem.
ASRSN:2121885.s: The flight crew descending for a visual approach to BOI 28L received a GPWS terrain caution at 4,200 feet due to selecting an MCP altitude of 4,000 feet while distracted by traffic. The pilot corrected the descent, attributing the error to misinterpreting the approach plate's terrain profile and missing prior safety notices.

ASRSN:2121903.n: Crew called via satellite phone reported. They were given a climbed to FL310. When the started the climb they heard a loud pop then got a left engine fire EICAS message. Followed checklist. Pulled the fire extinguisher bottle message went away. Reported they had shut the engine down. Wanted patch with Maintenance Control. And plan return to ZZZ. Flt had been airborne approx 30-40 mins. I gave the crew landing runway limit weight along with performance limits weight. We discussed dumping fuel vs landing overweight. Everyone agreed to dump fuel to be lighter for landing. Flight landed safely back in ZZZ. Did land approximately 10.0 overweight. Flight did not delay arrival to dump more fuel since we were under runway and performance limit. Since not 100 percent sure what happened to engine.[Requested priority]. Equipment rolled in ZZZ. My only concern here is crew called into Chief Pilot. I had asked to speak with crew if they called them 1st. Was not patched into crew or crew was not transferred to me. I ended up having the Chief Pilot call the Captain back and request he call me for fuel dump info. And for brief of event. Captain did call and irregular message completed.
ASRSN:2121903.s: The flight crew experienced a left engine fire warning and loud pop while climbing to FL310, shutting down the engine and returning to ZZZ. They landed safely approximately 10.0 overweight after deciding against further fuel dumping, though the specific engine failure cause remains unknown.

ASRSN:2121910.n: This report is submitted in accordance with Pilot Bulletin. We experienced GPS jamming, no spoofing, in the HECC FIR, Cairo, briefly in the vicinity of DATOK, then continuously from TAKSU through the OJAC FIR boundary. After landing in OJAI, we were jammed on the ground.All pilot bulletin and operations alert guidance followed.
ASRSN:2121910.s: Pilots reported GPS jamming without spoofing in the HECC FIR near DATOK and continuously from TAKSU through the OJAC boundary, continuing on the ground after landing in OJAI. The crew confirmed they followed all Pilot Bulletin and operations alert guidance.

ASRSN:2121927.n: Received a vector outside of ZZZZZ that appeared to give us a short final (for the visual) to Runway XXR. The winds were 20 kts stronger above 1500 feet and, unrecognized from me, pushed us to intercept the final course just outside the FAF. While worrying about working to correct the potential to be too high and the ability to get lower and configure in time, I over corrected and drove an approach in from 1300 feet AGL to approximately 1000 feet AGL from the vicinity of the FAF. As we were picking up the PAPIs tower came to our aid and informed us of our low approach. At this time (approximately 1300 AGL and fully configured) I disconnected the autopilot and auto throttle and flew the rest of the approach off the PAPIs / visual.Additional Details: Multiple delays and rescheduling of events in and around ZZZ added an element of fatigue to the crew. These delays also caused the flight crew to miss previously coordinated / scheduled meals.
ASRSN:2121927.s: The flight crew experienced fatigue from delays while flying a visual approach to Runway XXR. Strong winds above 1500 feet caused an overcorrection that resulted in a low approach from 1300 to 1000 feet AGL, prompting the pilot to disconnect automation and fly visually after tower notification.

ASRSN:2121929.n: We followed the latest guidance prior to entering affected airspace per company publications and pilot bulletins. We did experience several GPS spoofing events during descent and arrival resulting in ADS-B and TERR EICAS messages. From 200' AGL to exiting the runway after landing, we experienced constant EGPWS anomalous terrain warnings. During those 15 seconds, I obtained verbal confirmation from all three other pilots that these were anomalous warnings so we disregarded them. We had not disabled these warnings as they had not occurred prior to 200' during the descent and the guidance allows deselection at Captain's discretion. We followed procedure per the bulletin after parking to reselect GPS updating and deselect VOR-DME updating. There were no residual status messages associated with these events.
ASRSN:2121929.s: The flight crew experienced GPS spoofing during descent and arrival, causing ADS-B and TERR EICAS messages and constant EGPWS terrain warnings from 200' AGL to runway exit. The pilots verified the warnings were anomalous, disregarded them per guidance, and reset GPS updating after landing with no residual status messages.

ASRSN:2121962.n: A few seconds after setting the parking brake and checking visually (indicator and position) and by feel, the parking brake inadvertently released as my attention was on the remainder of the flow items. The FO noticed the airplane rolling backwards and I pressed the brakes. After the passengers were seated, the aircraft was tugged back into the correct position. I tested the parking brake several times and the issue was not repeated.I believe the pin that retains parking brake in the up position was not fully seated, and rather than being locked in, on this actuation was relying on friction to stay locked. I should have more firmly checked the security of the parking brake rather than rely on the fact that it had not fallen when I lowered my hand.In the future I will more firmly check the security of the parking brake against its locking mechanism to ensure that it is fully locked. After arriving in the ramp area and being marshaled into the gate, the marshaller made the signal to stop moving. I heard the Captain set the parking break and I turned the transponder to standby. I then grabbed the checklist in anticipation of the shutdown checklist call from the captain when I noticed movement which looked like the gate moving forward or us rolling backwards. I then told the captain to reengage the parking break due to it not being in the set position anymore. The ramp crew towed us forward and we ran the shutdown checklist.Cause: The parking break no being properly secured and confirmed engaged before the continuation of the shutdown flow.Suggestions: Scan the ON indication of the emergency break when the aircraft is at the gate and the parking break is pulled up to be engaged.
ASRSN:2121962.s: The First Officer reported that the parking brake inadvertently released during the shutdown flow at the gate because the retaining pin was not fully seated. The aircraft rolled backward until the Captain re-engaged the brakes, after which ramp crew towed it back into position.

ASRSN:2121988.n: After push/pull from the gate, we started ENG #1. We set brakes, and told the tug driver Brakes set…cleared to disconnect inter phone." Unbeknownst to us, immediately after ENG #1 completed its start cycle, the parking brakes failed. We started to very slowly drift forward. For a moment I thought it was an optical illusion. I looked at the parking brake and it was still set. The tug driver screamed "STOP, THE PLANE IS MOVING". I forcefully applied the toe brakes and we came to an unusually smooth slow stop. Right at that moment my First Officer (FO) pointed to the accumulator pressure gauge and it was reading"0"! We assumed that the smooth stop might have been that the accumulator pressure was already near zero when I applied the toe brakes. I kept pressure on the brakes until a Super Tug could be hooked up to our aircraft and tug us to a gate. We spoke to line maintenance and Maintenance Control while waiting to be tugged back in and went through steps with Maintenance control to restore braking. Recycling the nose wheel switch had no effect on accumulator pressure but recycling the parking brake did. Unfortunately, the pressure fell back to zero fairly quickly. Maintenance control mentioned some sort of Technical Standard Order (TSO) issue they were working regarding brakes but I wasn't clear as to exactly how that applied to our situation. We returned to the gate and Maintenance control took the aircraft out of service Cause: In our post event debrief I told my FO I was surprised that we didn't hit the tug and how fortunate that was! He told me that the tug appeared to be clear to aircraft right when we started drifting and that she apparently was still attached to the aircraft by the com line. I'm pretty certain that's not in keeping with SOP's but in this case, it was a fortunate mistake for us, as she was the one who alerted us to the fact that we were drifting. As for us, I obviously couldn't help but wonder if I checked the triple indicator carefully enough before engine start or if complacency had been a factor. After realizing that the inbound crew parked the aircraft without incident, the FO and I checking it during our preflight flows and the troubleshooting steps with Maintenance control, it was unlikely that we missed it and it was just a failure without any warning!" During pushback, the Captain set the brakes once the push was complete. We had started one engine, as the tug crew pulled away, the plane started to roll. We heard the ground crew still connected on headset yell out and scream, stop stop stop. The Captain proceeded to apply manual brake pressure. I immediately looked at the brake pressure accumulator which showed 0. No damage to the aircraft occurred. We proceeded working with Maintenance control, line maintenance, ops and ramp to get the aircraft tugged back to the gate. Cause: Mechanical issue
ASRSN:2121988.s: During pushback after starting Engine 1, the aircraft drifted forward due to a parking brake failure and zero accumulator pressure. The tug driver alerted the crew, allowing the Captain to stop the aircraft with toe brakes; no damage occurred, but the aircraft was taken out of service for a mechanical issue.

ASRSN:2122034.n: Prior our descent to ZZZ we had a master caution indication and an ECAM message for Smoke: avionics smoke. Then we performed the ECAM actions, [advised ATC] and we both decided to divert to ZZZ1. We had no indication of smoke or fumes inside the cockpit nor the cabin. As soon as we turned to ZZZ1 the ECAM message disappeared and since we were close to initiating the descent to ZZZ we decided to cancel the [priority handling] and continue to ZZZ. Later, during the descent to ZZZ and approximately 10 minutes after the indication went out, we had the ECAM avionics smoke message again. [Requested priority handling] one more time, running the ECAM and flying fast to get the aircraft on the ground as soon as possible. After an assessment we decided to continue to ZZZ. The Captain informed the company, flight attendants (FAs) and the passengers of the situation. Once on ground a firefighter team checked the aircraft for any smoke indication, the passengers were well aware of what was happening. After the inspection we continued to the assigned parking spot, deplaning the aircraft normally. Ground personnel also checked the avionics compartment. This was the last flight as part of my IOE.
ASRSN:2122034.s: The flight crew experienced a recurring avionics smoke ECAM message during descent to ZZZ, prompting a temporary diversion to ZZZ1 before returning to ZZZ. After landing, ground personnel inspected the aircraft and avionics compartment, finding no smoke, allowing for normal deplaning.

ASRSN:2122040.n: On departure, just prior to leveling at three thousand, received master warning and Right Bleed Fail annunciator light. I continued to fly and second in command (SIC) requested delay vectors to work the problem, remaining at three thousand. SIC accomplished the QRH procedure and confirmed Right bleed shutoff and mode selector shut off with me. We informed ZZZ Approach of our decision to return to ZZZ. Person A did an excellent job of coordinating with ATC and company as well as loading an approach to Runway XX Left in a very short period of time. Total flight time for all of above was 18 minutes takeoff to touchdown.Cause: Right bleed air leak. Leak detector functioned as advertised.Suggestions: Bleed air leak detection system worked perfectly, I am not aware of any maintenance procedure or test that can detect a faulty bleed valve on the ground.
ASRSN:2122040.s: The pilot and second in command experienced a Right Bleed Fail warning on departure just before leveling at 3,000 feet. They returned to ZZZ Airport after confirming a right bleed air leak, landing 18 minutes after takeoff.

ASRSN:2122060.n: Low altitude alert. While flying the ILS 6 at TEB we experienced the LOC fluctuating 1-1.5 dots left and right outside of DANDY. Conditions were VFR and the airport was in sight. The Autopilot was on and it started to chase the needles. This monopolized my attention and led to a degradation of SA. I almost missed the 1500 altitude restriction at DANDY, but the second in command (SIC) reminded when I failed to start the descent. At this point I disengaged the Autopilot and initiated a descent. Crossing DANDY the received a 'low altitude alert' from the Tower and I observed the altitude at 1400. I corrected the altitude and continued the approach in visual conditions. Circling to land Runway 1. I did not receive a brasher warning from TEB Tower but I was expecting it. After landing I observed men and equipment working on Runway 6 directly in front of the LOC antenna. We reported the issues with the LOC signal to Ground Control. Another plane overheard our transmission and reported to Tower that they had also experienced fluctuations. The LOC frequency has very recently been changed at TEB as well.
ASRSN:2122060.s: The pilot flying an ILS 6 approach at TEB experienced Localizer fluctuations causing Autopilot oscillation and a missed 1500-foot descent at DANDY, resulting in a low altitude alert at 1400 feet. The crew attributed the signal instability to runway maintenance near the antenna and a recent frequency change.

ASRSN:2122061.n: During a training flight the hydraulic pump caution light illuminated, followed by the landing gear master warning CAS (Crew Alert System) message. I took controls and the student and I used the checklist to diagnose the problem and performed an emergency gear extension. ZZZ approach was notified and we returned to ZZZ [airport]. For extra caution we did a low approach for tower to confirm that the main gear was down and locked. After the low approach we returned for a normal landing without injury or damage to the aircraft.
ASRSN:2122061.s: During a training flight, a hydraulic pump caution and landing gear master warning prompted the pilot and student to perform an emergency gear extension. After notifying ZZZ approach and confirming gear status via a low approach, the aircraft landed normally without injury or damage.

ASRSN:2122108.n: A passenger was required to check their carry on bag because of bag space running out. They forgot to remove a pair of headphones in a charging case and informed me. I informed the FA1 who informed the gate agents and captain. The agents insisted that it did not count as a lithium ion battery and told the FA1 that only removable suitcase batteries could not be checked. They also stated that they did not want to remove the bag because we were at departure time and they did not want the flight to be further delayed. We took off with a lithium ion battery in our cargo hold and the bag is supposed to be checked on to ZZZZ putting passengers at even more risk.The airline puts a lot of pressure on gate agents to push flights out on time. They are threatening their jobs if flights are delayed, even if they are not personally responsible. This is leading to FARs being broken and passengers are being put at risk.
ASRSN:2122108.s: Gate agents overruled the flight attendant and captain to check a bag containing a lithium-ion battery, citing departure pressure and job security. The aircraft departed with the prohibited item in the cargo hold, violating regulations and increasing risk to passengers.

ASRSN:2122141.n: Landed aircraft at ZZZ [airport]. Upon rollout I applied power to taxi off the runway and the engine died and would not restart. We eventually had to push the plane off the runway. The plane restarted 15 minutes later when back at the hangar.This was a delivery of a newly purchased aircraft from ZZZ1 [airport] to ZZZ [airport]. The aircraft had been mostly idle for the few years prior to the event.I suspect the following possibilities: Carburetor icing. I applied carburetor heat during the descent and landing but it may have been ineffective. Both fuel tanks were exactly at 1/4 tank. Cessna 120/140 aircraft have a warning about takeoff with less than 1/4 tank.I also discovered, post flight, that the transponder had not inspected within required time period. When checking the logbooks, I noted the entry for installing ADS-B out but did not check for transponder sign-off. On online ADS-B data (I know not official) I did see a prior flight with what looked like reasonable altitude. After landing, engine stopped on runway for undetermined reason. I recently purchased the aircraft and verified that ADS-B transmitter was operational on which I focused to fly into the mode C vail. After landing at ZZZ [airport], determined that the aircraft transponder operation was not current and immediately contacted an A&P to complete currency requirements.
ASRSN:2122141.s: The pilot landed a newly purchased, idle Cessna 120/140 at ZZZ airport, where the engine died on rollout and required a pushback. The pilot suspects carburetor icing or low fuel as the cause and later discovered the transponder was not current.

ASRSN:2122142.n: While enroute IFR to ZZZ [airport], my No 1 Nav/com, an Avidyne IFD440, went off line with Red Xs on the VHF portion. I smelled a burning electrical smell, and later learned that the Circuit breaker had popped. I [advised ATC], established communications with ATC on 121.5 using my number two radio. I diverted to the nearest airport, ZZZ1, and cleared to land, which I did uneventfully. I removed the radio from the tray, and detected a burning smell inside the radio. I inspected the aircraft carefully for any electrical anomalies or burning, including by removing the cowl, and inspecting the tray. I reset the circuit breaker, which did not pop. The fire crew on the ground used their infrared thermometer and detected no unusual heat, or burning, within the aircraft. I flew back to ZZZ2 [airport] without incident using the no. 2 Nav/comm with a handheld radio available in case it was needed. On the following day, Day 1, I arranged for an aircraft mechanic to inspect the plane, which occurred Day 2. The mechanic reported no anomalies or discrepancies with the aircraft and authorized continued flights..
ASRSN:2122142.s: The pilot experienced a No 1 Avidyne IFD440 Nav/com failure with a popped circuit breaker and burning smell while enroute IFR. After diverting to ZZZ1 for an uneventful landing and ground inspection, the pilot returned to ZZZ2 and received mechanic authorization for continued flight with no discrepancies found.

ASRSN:2122165.n: Airplane throttle became stuck at full throttle. The airplane had already been cleared to land when the condition was identified. ATC was notified of the condition and the possibility of the airplane being disabled on the runway. No further assistance was needed. A power off landing was made and the airplane was able to clear the runway with remaining speed. Airplane was disabled on taxiway and was towed by company maintenance moments later. ATC was notified by pilot of condition of airplane and pilot signed off the frequency until maintenance arrived.
ASRSN:2122165.s: The pilot reported a throttle stuck at full power during the landing phase after receiving landing clearance. A power-off landing was executed, allowing the aircraft to clear the runway before being disabled on a taxiway and towed by maintenance.

ASRSN:2122171.n: On Day 0 at approximately XA:55 hours I had just leveled the aircraft at FL250 per ATC request. I heard a loud bang and vibrations coming from the right engine of the CE680. I confirmed with my copilot and the engine instruments that we had a right engine failure. My copilot [requested priority handling] and stated that we had an engine failure to ATC. ATC failed to acknowledge my copilots request. My copilot [requested priority handling] a second time and the ATC continued to give other aircraft instructions. It was not until an airline pilot instructed ATC to answer our call that our [priority handling] was acknowledged. During this time I confirmed the right engine had failed and the ITT (Interstage Turbine Temperature) was still climbing. I had the copilot confirm this information. I brought the right throttle to idle. The ITT continued to climb. I shutdown the right engine by moving the right throttle to the fuel cutoff detent. The ITT decreased on the right engine. At this time my copilot was able to communicate with ATC and a decent and heading to the south was given for a planned runway X arrival at ZZZ. The engine shutdown checklist was completed and the single engine approach checklist was completed. The decent, arrival and landing were uneventful on a single engine. We requested the firetrucks be available on arrival. I briefly stopped on the runway in front of the fire trucks to confirm that there was not a fire. After no fire was confirmed I taxied to the FBO followed by the firetrucks. After shutdown on the ramp I met with the fire fighters who inspected the aircraft and determined no reportable damage was observed. I met with an official who took a picture of my pilot license and took my contact information for his report. As of this report an engine inspection by the manufacture is planned but not started.
ASRSN:2122171.s: The pilot of a CE680 experienced a right engine failure at FL250, marked by a loud bang and rising ITT. After ATC initially ignored priority requests, the crew shut down the engine, landed safely on one engine, and confirmed no fire or reportable damage.

ASRSN:2122182.n: During a Part 91 private flight from HECA, significant GPS jamming and subsequently, GPS spoofing was encountered within both the Nicosia and Ankara FIR boundaries. The loss of GPS satellite coverage on both GPS 1 and 2 initially occurred abeam RNAV waypoint TUVLO at FL400, M.82. The time of the initial GPS jamming was approximately at XA55. Prior to departure the crew had discussed the potential threat of GPS interference enroute, the Captain had already experienced it several times in the region in the preceding month. The first indication was loss of ADS-B, followed by successive loss of VOR and VOR/DME. Nicola ATC were notified of the occurrence, but the IRS (Inertial Reference System) navigation was maintaining the FMS routing. However, on entering the Ankara FIR, the GPS jamming became GPS spoofing. The left-seat PIC (PM) PFD (Primary Flight Display) displayed a 200 nm confirmed position error. The right-seat SIC (Second in Command) (PF) PFD continued to display accurate position information. However, the lack of the ability for the IRS systems to update from the GPS led to dead-reckoning mode and predicted fuel errors. Furthermore, it also appeared that the ground or more likely, airborne military GPS jamming was also affecting ground VOR/DME stations. As a result, radar headings were requested from Ankara ATC. At approximately XB20 both PFDs showed a magenta background and a spurious EGPWS 'TERRAIN PULL UP!' audio and visual alert occurred. The EGPWS was selected off to cancel the alert. The GPS spoofing continued for 2 hours, until it was within the BAKU FIR. At night, in unfamiliar airspace and at a lower altitude, this could have been a far more serious situation.
ASRSN:2122182.s: During a Part 91 flight at FL400, the crew encountered GPS jamming and spoofing in Nicosia and Ankara FIRs, causing ADS-B/VOR loss, position errors, and false EGPWS alerts. The crew maintained IRS navigation and requested radar headings from Ankara ATC until the interference ceased in the Baku FIR.

ASRSN:2122183.n: Just after takeoff, landing gear horn and warning lights came on. On climbout, I accepted a vector from ZZZ tower and was instructed to contact ZZZ departure. Because the horn was still blaring, I asked tower if I could stay with local control until I could work out the issue with the landing gear. I offered to fly east of the airport to avoid interference with traffic in the pattern. After turning east, I was asked by the tower controller if I wanted to cancel my IFR clearance. I canceled IFR with the controller. After cycling the landing gear a couple of times, I thought that it was working correctly, but the horn and warning lights were not showing a safe condition. I asked tower for a low approach so that they could look at the state of the landing gear. My request was approved, and I was told I could overfly taxiway 1 to be closer to the tower. The tower controller said the landing gear appeared down, so I requested a landing on runway XX. The tower approved and rolled emergency equipment. I went around the traffic pattern and landed uneventfully.I taxied to the ramp and thanked the emergency responders and the tower controllers.
ASRSN:2122183.s: The pilot experienced a landing gear warning horn and lights just after takeoff. After canceling IFR and performing a low approach for visual confirmation, the pilot landed uneventfully on runway XX with emergency equipment rolled.

ASRSN:2122189.n: While training takeoffs and landings at ZZZ [airport], a Sikorsky S-76 landed on the approach end of runway XX. After announcing our position on base, the Sikorsky S-76 announced they were taking off and we had the traffic in sight so we continued onto final approach. The helicopter took significantly longer than expected after announcing they were taking off, so we then side stepped to the right and after configuring for a go-around, announced our intentions to go-around. The Sikorsky S-76 eventually departed the runway and we flew approximately 100 feet laterally on the departure leg of the pattern abeam them while we performed our go-around. Communications were made after the incident with the pilot of the Sikorsky S-76 to clarify what had happened and to help ensure future safety.
ASRSN:2122189.s: A training aircraft and a Sikorsky S-76 helicopter at ZZZ airport experienced a runway incursion when the helicopter delayed departure after announcing takeoff. The training pilot executed a go-around and side-stepped right, passing 100 feet laterally abeam the helicopter before the helicopter cleared the runway.

ASRSN:2122193.n: I was training a CFI initial applicant in his Arrow Aircraft X. We were doing many maneuvers between ZZZ1 and ZZZ2. On initiating a slow flight demo I noticed that the gear didn't deploy. Tried cycling a couple of times and then decided to stop the lesson and return to ZZZ. I gave control to the my student (PIC) of the flight and I'd run coms. As we returned to hooks we analyzed the situation and decided to 'blow' the gear down. I began the checklist and process. Got gear down and three green. Then we discussed further plans on how we'd talk to tower and get a low approach. I looked up and noticed we were over Location X and Y was in sight. From being a local instructor of about 5 years I knew exactly were we were. We were in ZZZ2's airspace. I commanded an immediate right turn to exit ZZZ2's delta airspace. We continued the flight to ZZZ, did the low approach to confirm gear down and landed without incident.Main reason for the violation is distraction due to the [priority handling] situation. As the CFI and overall ranking PIC I should have had better situational awareness of what airspace of we might be going in. I was receiving training for CFI initial in equity owned partnership PA28R-200 Aircraft X.We were doing practice maneuvers between ZZZ1 and ZZZ2. When initiating a slow flight demo, landing gear did not extend. Tried to cycle gear with no success. Aborted the maneuver, and stopped the lesson. I assumed control of the aircraft and instructor assumed comms.Started running checklist and determined return to ZZZ was best option. After checking breakers and placing gear control to down again, with sharp pitch change was able to get 3 green gear indication. Discussed further plans on on how to return to ZZZ and communicate to tower the situation and request fly by to verify gear down position when noticed we where about to enter ZZZ2 class D airspace. Was under ZZZ3 bravo shelf at 1500 ft. Made immediate west turn to exit airspace but clipped ZZZ2 D airspace.Continued flight to ZZZ and did the low approach to confirm gear down. Tower confirmed gear down and landed after the fly-by without incident.Reason for the airspace violation is distraction due the [priority handling] situation.Should have had better situational awareness of aircraft position in relation to ZZZ2 airspace.
ASRSN:2122193.s: A CFI and student in a PA28R-200 experienced a landing gear malfunction during training between ZZZ1 and ZZZ2. Distraction from the emergency caused the crew to inadvertently enter ZZZ2 Class D airspace at 1,500 feet before correcting course and landing safely.

ASRSN:2122195.n: While several flight school aircraft were operating in the pattern at ZZZ [airport] for runway XX the AWOS was reporting winds calm, however we noted through both the windsock and aircraft performance that the wind was really favoring runway XY and we were landing with a marginal tailwind. All flight school C172s (a total of 3 at the time) discussed over CTAF and reorganized to join a pattern for runway XY without issue. On a touch and go myself and my student noticed a twin Aerostar taxi without any radio calls to the departure end of XX and noted the possible risk of a runway incursion. He held short and we continued left traffic. Another flight school aircraft was turning approximately a 3/4 mile final and announced it over CTAF. Immediately after the Aerostar makes a radio call along the lines of 'Aerostar departing runway XX, the CORRECT runway if any of you could actually use this cool tool called a windsock on the ground and paid any attention' in a very aggressive tone. The aircraft on final immediately repeated that they were on short final XY, to which the Aerostar announced 'I'm already on the correct runway that the wind is favoring so get go around and deal with it'. From our position in the downwind we could clearly see he was at least 5-10 feet short of the hold short line and still stopped even after his call, but elected to enter the runway anyway. His departure path came closely under the final traffic, right behind traffic that was crossing midfield to join the downwind, and right over a helicopter entering the pattern. Each aircraft had limited room to maneuver but fortunately all were highly aware and able to avoid. The Aerostar made a few more snide replies about no one but him being able to read a windsock before departing the area. We continued our lap in the pattern after his departure and noted the windsock showed nearly no wind, barely a slight breeze favoring XY.
ASRSN:2122195.s: A flight school C172 pilot reported that an Aerostar pilot aggressively entered runway XX against windsock indications, forcing a near-miss with traffic on final for runway XY. The Aerostar pilot's refusal to hold short and confrontational radio calls created a runway incursion risk, though all aircraft avoided collision through situational awareness.

ASRSN:2122197.n: We were on with ZZZ tower coming back in to land at ZZZ when tower gave us a traffic alert for two Military Fighter Jets that were within 300' of us and told us to immediately turn. We did and got more separation from them. Within 5 minutes tower gave us a second traffic alert for a 172 that was having ADSB issues that was at our altitude and heading straight for us. We had to do evasive maneuvers both times to get away from the traffic. We were approximately 8 miles east of the airport when this all occurred.
ASRSN:2122197.s: The pilot reported two traffic alerts while approaching ZZZ airport, first from military fighter jets within 300 feet and then from a Cessna 172 with ADSB issues at the same altitude. Evasive maneuvers were required both times to avoid collision approximately 8 miles east of the airport.

ASRSN:2122200.n: On Day 0 myself, was flying my drone over Beverly Hills, CA for a commercial photo mission. I had authorization to fly at XB:45 pm up to 400 ft. for 1hr as per LAANC ALTXXXXXXXXX authorization and a LAANC Authorization ALTXXXXXXXXY to fly up to 200 ft. starting at XA:13pm for 2hrs.But due to my own negligence I started to climb up to 400 ft. at XA:38pm for 1 minute and then descended back down to 200 ft. and did the same maneuver at XA:38pm for 1 minute. I was distracted by some tourists who asked about my mission and while explaining things to them, pointing out the drone and letting them see my monitor, I didn't pay attention to the fact that my clearance for 400 ft. was only given after XB:45pm and I started climbing above the permitted altitude of 200 ft. for that time frame.I discovered it when I started my dusk shoot at XC:00 pm by recalling my XB:45pm authorization.There was no aircraft traffic in the area and I was mainly flying over buildings, so no real safety concerns arose. I had visual line-of-sight to my drone at all times.What I learned from this situation was that I should not let myself get distracted by curious people when flying a drone.
ASRSN:2122200.s: A commercial drone pilot violated LAANC altitude clearances by climbing to 400 ft. before the authorized time due to distraction from tourists. The pilot realized the error later, noting no aircraft traffic was present and no safety concerns arose.

ASRSN:2122203.n: I was flying my drone near Waikiki beach for personal use. I wanted to keep the scenic view of the beach. I use the drone's app and AirHub Portal for flight planning and authorization if necessary. For this mission, I was clear of any controlled airspace and the approval was not required. After flying my drone for about 15 minutes, I was done with the mission. I reviewed the fly path through the app and realized that I was very close to PHNL airspace. I kept the drone under 50 feet for the most part but for a minute I was over 100 feet. Requesting the authorization could have been more safe operation for me and others whether it was necessary or not. Getting more familiar with the airspace and geographic location could have been helpful, especially since it was my first time being there.
ASRSN:2122203.s: A drone operator flew a personal mission near Waikiki Beach, briefly exceeding 100 feet and operating close to PHNL airspace without authorization. The operator concluded that requesting approval and gaining better local airspace familiarity would have improved safety.

ASRSN:2122207.n: Training in process. Traffic was very slow and we had just taken over the sector. Aircraft X was at 140. The route was the ZZZZZ arrival. Normally this would be in the scratch pad but for some reason it wasn't. I'm not sure if the previous controller took it out or if it wasn't in there from the center. The hand off to the next sector for this aircraft should have been 130. The trainee assumed the aircraft was on V388 and descended to 100. I did not catch that the trainee descended to 100 and the aircraft went into an 110 MVA. The next sector caught it and let me know.This trainee has well over 200 hours training on this combined sector. I let myself not become complacent because there was very light traffic. I should have been more engaged.
ASRSN:2122207.s: An air traffic controller and trainee managed Aircraft X on the ZZZZZ arrival during training. The trainee incorrectly descended the aircraft to 100, causing an 110 MVA, which the controller attributed to complacency due to light traffic.

ASRSN:2122212.n: Aircraft X was cleared for ILS Runway 12 with a restriction to cross KICDO at 10,000. I noticed that well before getting to KICDO the aircraft started an unexpected, incompliant turn. I called attention to it to the pilot and offered vectors for the approach. Then seemed confused and asked for the vector. I issued a vector and reassigned 10000. The aircraft was in a 10,000 MVA. Readback was good. I moved to other tasks. I then noticed they had descended below the assigned altitude and below the MVA. At this point the aircraft was entering a lower MVA so I reassigned a new altitude compliant with the new MVA, but the Loss was too late to recover. After establishing them on the approach I issued the brasher statement. I have had numerous aircraft take the early turn prior to KICDO. I have never had one descend until now.
